doc.title: Mose Allison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Evolving songwriting and borrowed styles; looking for the song in the book
summary: Panken notes growing complexity; Audre reads Collingwood on artists borrowing.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: We’re getting an empirical demonstration of how your conception of songwriting was evolving and becoming more complex, the more you were singing... And you were probably listening to what other people were doing, too, and absorbing that into what you were thinking about.
Yeah. Well...
“All artists have modeled their style upon that of others, used subjects that others have used, and treated them as others have treated them already.” That’s one of the things in here...
You’re reading from the Collingwood book now.
Yes.
I think a lot of them are very...they’re universal themes and kind of philosophical, but they’re funny. They’re all kind of pithy remarks that are down-home and funny.
Or surprising.
“Everybody Cryin’ Mercy.”
Yeah. That’s on this one, Dad.
Do you still sing “Everybody’s Crying Mercy.”
Yeah, I still sing...
What number in the book is it?
What number is it?
In the book. Do you know what number it is, Dad?
For the bass player?
Not in the lyrics. In that book...
When you tell the bass player that you’re going to play it...
“If You’re Goin’ To the City”... You know, one of my favorites is “City Home.”
“If You’re Goin’ To The City” is a wonderful song.
That’s true. That’s a different one. But yeah...
